summary:
Every crew has a weakest member. For worker `i` as the weakest, the sum only grows as the crew widens, so the
best such crew stretches until a strictly weaker worker on each side. Monotonic stacks find those boundaries
for every worker, prefix sums give each crew's total, and the answer is the best `strength[i] × sum`. O(n).

question.md:
A crew is a run of neighbouring workers; its power is (weakest strength) × (total strength). Return the largest
power over all crews.

- **Strengths are positive**, so adding a worker never lowers the sum, though it may lower the minimum.
- **Up to 10⁵ workers with strength up to 10⁶**: a sum reaches 10¹¹ and a power 10¹⁷, which needs 64-bit
  integers (still below 9.2 × 10¹⁸).

think.md:
Strengths `[3, 1, 6, 4, 5, 2]`. The crew `6, 4, 5` has weakest 4 and total 15: power 60. The whole row has weakest 1
and total 21: power 21. The best is **60**, from the crew
2..4 with weakest worker 3.

Group crews by their weakest member. If worker `i` is the weakest, widening the crew (while keeping `i` the
weakest) only adds positive strengths, so the widest such crew is best. It reaches until the nearest strictly
weaker worker on each side. So the answer is the best of `n` candidates, and each needs the nearest weaker
neighbours (monotonic stacks) and a range sum (prefix sums).

approaches.title: Every crew, with running minimum and sum

idea.md: For each first worker, extend the crew to the right, updating the weakest strength and the total; each crew's power is their product.

build: For each end `j`: update both and compare `low × sum` with the best.

lines.text: Crews starting at worker `i`; the total is 64-bit.
Add worker `j`: the weakest may drop, the total grows.

steps.text: Start at worker 0: powers [9, 4, 10, 14, 19, 21] for crews ending at 0..5.
Start at worker 1: powers [1, 7, 11, 16, 18] for crews ending at 1..5.
Start at worker 2: powers [36, 40, 60, 34] for crews ending at 2..5.
Start at worker 3: powers [16, 36, 22] for crews ending at 3..5.
Start at worker 4: powers [25, 14] for crews ending at 4..5.
Start at worker 5: powers [4] for crews ending at 5..5.

walk.title: Every crew: fix the first worker, extend to the right, keeping the weakest strength and the running sum.

limits.md: ~5 × 10⁹ crews for 10⁵ workers. Only one crew per weakest worker can be the best (the widest), so n candidates suffice.

approaches.title: Widest crew per weakest worker

idea.md: Prefix sums `P`. With a stack, find for each worker the nearest strictly weaker worker on the left (`left[i]` = the index after it) and on the right (`right[i]` = the index before it). Worker `i`'s candidate power is `strength[i] × (P[right[i] + 1] − P[left[i]])`. Return the largest.

build: Left pass (pop while `≥`): `left[i]` = after the nearest weaker worker, or 0.
Right pass (pop while `≥`): `right[i]` = before the nearest weaker worker, or `n − 1`.

lines.text: Prefix sums, so any crew's total is one subtraction (64-bit: up to 10¹¹).
Nearest strictly weaker worker on the left, via a stack of increasing strengths; the crew can start right after it (or at 0).

The same from the right: the crew can end right before the nearest strictly weaker worker (or at `n − 1`). Equal strengths don't stop the crew; a tied weakest member just gives the same crew twice, which is harmless for a maximum.
Worker `i` as the weakest of its widest crew. The multiplication happens in 64 bits because the sum is 64-bit.

complexity.md: **Time O(n):** prefix sums plus two stack passes. **Space O(n).**

steps.text: Prefix sums: the crew l..r sums to P[r + 1] − P[l].
Worker 0 (strength 3) as the weakest: crew 0..0, sum 3, power 3 × 3 = 9.
Worker 1 (strength 1) as the weakest: crew 0..5, sum 21, power 1 × 21 = 21.
Worker 2 (strength 6) as the weakest: crew 2..2, sum 6, power 6 × 6 = 36.
Worker 3 (strength 4) as the weakest: crew 2..4, sum 15, power 4 × 15 = 60.
Worker 4 (strength 5) as the weakest: crew 4..4, sum 5, power 5 × 5 = 25.
Worker 5 (strength 2) as the weakest: crew 2..5, sum 17, power 2 × 17 = 34.

walk.title: The best crew with weakest member i spreads as far as possible: until a weaker worker on each side. Stacks find those boundaries, prefix sums give the crew's total.

takeaways.md:
- **min × sum over subarrays:** fix the minimum; with positive values, the widest subarray around it is best.
- Nearest smaller on each side (monotonic stacks) + prefix sums = O(n).
- For a maximum, ties can be counted twice; for a sum over subarrays (like the stretch-lows problem), they can't.
